q: The tiny extra pocket inside the front-right pocket of jeans was originally made to hold what?
note: Levi's still calls it the watch pocket; today it mostly holds coins or keys.

q: Why were ridged edges first put on gold and silver coins?
a: To stop people shaving metal off
options: To stop people shaving metal off
To help people count them in the dark
To make them easier to stack
note: Clipping precious metal from smooth-edged coins was once a common crime.

q: The abbreviation 'lb' for a pound comes from which Latin word?
note: The £ sign for money is a stylised L from the same Latin word.

q: The QWERTY keyboard layout was first designed in the 1870s for which machine?
note: American inventor Christopher Latham Sholes developed the layout.

q: What are the small raised bumps on the F and J keys of a keyboard for?
a: Finding the home row without looking
options: Finding the home row without looking
note: Touch typists rest their index fingers on those two keys.

q: What is the tiny hole near the bottom of an aeroplane cabin window for?
note: This 'breather hole' also helps stop the window from fogging up.

q: What does the distress signal SOS actually stand for?
note: It was adopted as the international standard at a 1906 radiotelegraph convention.

q: The radio distress call 'Mayday' comes from a phrase in which language?
note: It echoes the French 'm'aider', meaning 'help me'.

q: Barcodes registered through GS1 India begin with which three-digit prefix?
note: The prefix shows where a barcode was registered, not where the product was made.

q: On most payment cards, what is the last digit of the long card number?
note: It is worked out with the Luhn formula to catch typing mistakes.

q: A payment card number beginning with the digit 4 belongs to which network?
note: American Express card numbers begin with 34 or 37.

q: By the Rule of 72, money growing at 8% a year doubles in roughly how many years?
note: Divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate to estimate the doubling time.

q: The huge-number word 'googol' was coined by the nine-year-old nephew of which American mathematician?
note: Kasner made the word famous in his 1940 book 'Mathematics and the Imagination'.

q: Wi-Fi is often said to mean 'Wireless Fidelity'. What did the name stand for when it was coined?
note: Branding firm Interbrand coined it as a catchy nod to 'hi-fi'.

q: What is the little dot over a lowercase 'i' or 'j' called?
note: It comes from Medieval Latin 'titulus', used for a small stroke written over letters.

q: What is the plastic tip at the end of a shoelace called?
note: It stops the lace fraying and makes threading it through eyelets easy.

q: What is the metal band that holds an eraser onto a pencil called?
note: The same word is used for the metal cap on the tip of a walking stick.

q: Pencil 'lead' contains no lead. What is it mainly made of?
note: Early users mistook graphite for a kind of lead, and the name stuck.

q: On a pencil, what do the letters HB stand for?
note: More H means harder and lighter; more B means softer and darker.

q: Why does a BIC pen cap have a small hole in its top?
a: To let air through if inhaled
options: To let air through if inhaled
To make it easier to grip
note: BIC says the vent meets international safety standards for pen caps.

q: The 'Save' icon in many apps is a picture of which old storage device?
note: The common 3.5-inch floppy held just 1.44 MB of data.

q: Clock faces with Roman numerals usually show the number four as what?
In most watch adverts, the hands are set to about what time?
note: The hands frame the brand logo and look a bit like a smile.

q: A calculator keypad has 7 8 9 on its top row. Which digits top a phone keypad?
note: Bell Labs tested push-button layouts before settling on 1-2-3 at the top.

q: Bubble wrap's inventors were originally trying to make what?
note: Its inventors later found it worked brilliantly as packaging.

q: Velcro was invented after an engineer noticed which prickly seed heads stuck to his dog's fur?
note: Swiss engineer George de Mestral patented his fastener in the 1950s.

q: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented work trousers in 1873 for adding what?
note: The rivets strengthened pocket corners that tore under heavy work.

q: The fabric name 'denim' comes from 'serge de' which French city?
note: 'Jeans' takes its name from Genoa, an Italian port famous for sturdy cotton cloth.

q: YKK, the letters stamped on many zips, is a company from which country?
note: YKK stands for Yoshida Kogyo Kabushikikaisha, after founder Tadao Yoshida.

q: Before it became a children's toy, Play-Doh was sold as what?
note: It was used to lift soot off wallpaper in coal-heated homes.

q: One knot, used for ship and aircraft speeds, equals one what per hour?
note: Sailors measured speed by counting knots on a rope let out behind the ship.

q: The word 'mile' comes from the Latin for 'a thousand' what?
note: A Roman pace was a double step, about five Roman feet.

q: In 'a.m.', which Latin phrase meaning 'before midday' is abbreviated?
note: 'p.m.' is short for 'post meridiem', meaning after midday.

q: How many loaves or rolls make a 'baker's dozen'?
note: Explanations vary: avoiding fines for short weight, or a free loaf as the reseller's cut.

q: What is the sum of all the whole numbers from 1 to 100?
note: Pair them up: 1+100, 2+99 and so on gives 50 pairs of 101.

q: Since 2007, how many digits does a standard ISBN book number have?
note: Older ISBNs had 10 digits and could end in the letter X.

q: Which word for a lucky accidental discovery did Horace Walpole coin in 1754?
note: He based it on a Persian fairy tale whose heroes kept making lucky discoveries.

q: Which English word for a powerful business person comes from the Japanese 'taikun', meaning great lord?
note: Foreigners used it in the 1850s as a title for Japan's military ruler.

q: Which one-piece gymnastics garment is named after a 19th-century French trapeze artist?
note: Jules Léotard also inspired the song 'The Daring Young Man on the Flying Trapeze'.

q: Which word for a dark outline image comes from an 18th-century French finance minister known for cost-cutting?
note: Why his name stuck is debated; the usual story links it to jokes about his austerity.

q: Which branch of maths gets its name from the Arabic 'al-jabr', meaning the restoring of broken parts?
note: It comes from the title of a 9th-century book by the Persian scholar al-Khwarizmi.

q: The English words 'zero' and 'cipher' both come from which Arabic word meaning empty?
note: Arab scholars used it to translate the Sanskrit 'shunya', meaning empty.

q: Which month's name comes from the Latin for 'eight', even though it is now the tenth month?
note: The early Roman calendar began in March, so this month really was eighth.

q: Wednesday is named after which Germanic god?
note: Friday likewise honours the goddess Frigg.

q: Which language gave English 'kindergarten', literally 'children's garden'?
note: Friedrich Fröbel opened his first one in 1837 and named it Kindergarten in 1840.

q: The word 'pixel' is short for 'picture' plus which other word?
note: Every digital photo is a grid of these tiny coloured squares.

q: The word 'muscle' comes from the Latin for a 'little' what, because a flexing muscle looked like one moving?
note: Latin 'musculus' means both small mouse and muscle.

q: The word 'clue' comes from 'clew', meaning a ball of what?
note: In Greek myth, Theseus followed a thread to find his way out of the labyrinth.

q: 'Window' comes from Old Norse 'vindauga', meaning 'wind' plus which body part?
note: Early windows were unglazed holes that let in wind as well as light.

q: The word 'bank' comes from the Italian 'banca', meaning what piece of furniture?
note: Renaissance Florentine bankers did business at benches covered with cloth.

q: 'Budget' comes from the old French 'bougette', a small leather what?
note: The money sense, from 1733, came from ministers keeping their financial plans in a wallet.

q: The word 'money' traces back to the temple of which Roman goddess, where coins were minted?
note: Her title 'Moneta' also gave English the word 'mint'.

q: The word 'quarantine' comes from the Italian for how many days?
note: Arriving crews had to wait that long before coming ashore.

q: The word 'dollar' comes from 'thaler', a silver coin first minted in a town now in which country?
note: Silver from Joachimsthal, today Jáchymov, made the 'Joachimsthaler' coin.

q: The word 'robot', from a 1920 Czech play, comes from a word meaning what?
note: Karel Čapek's play R.U.R. used it; his brother Josef suggested the word.

q: The word 'dinosaur', coined by Richard Owen in 1842, literally means what?
note: It comes from the Greek 'deinos', terrible, and 'sauros', lizard.

q: The word 'emoji' comes from Japanese words meaning what?
note: Despite the look-alike, it has nothing to do with the English word 'emotion'.

q: 'Checkmate' comes from the Persian 'shah mat'. What does 'shah' mean?
note: What 'mat' meant is debated: 'dead', 'helpless' or 'stunned'.

q: The word 'boycott' comes from Charles Boycott, who was what?
note: In 1880 his local community refused to work for him or trade with him.

q: A myth says 'kangaroo' meant 'I don't understand'. What is the truth?
a: It's an Aboriginal name for the animal
options: It's an Aboriginal name for the animal
note: In Guugu Yimithirr, 'gangurru' names a kind of large kangaroo; Cook's crew recorded it in 1770.

q: Linguist Allen Walker Read traced 'OK' to an 1839 joke abbreviation of what?
note: Newspapers of the time had a fad for abbreviating deliberate misspellings.

q: The word 'alphabet' joins the first two letters of which language's alphabet?
note: Alpha and beta became the Latin 'alphabetum'.

q: Which ancient region's base-60 counting gave us 60 minutes in an hour?
note: The same base-60 system gives us 60 seconds in a minute.

q: Which English word for thick, wild woodland comes, via Hindi, from a Sanskrit word that meant dry wasteland?
note: Sanskrit 'jangala' described arid, uncultivated land.

q: Which informal English word meaning easy and comfortable comes from the Hindi-Urdu 'khush'?
note: It began as British soldiers' slang, borrowed from Anglo-Indian speech.

q: Which English word for an expert commentator comes from the Sanskrit 'pandita', a learned person?
note: In English it first meant an Indian scholar, then any expert giving opinions.

q: Which twin-hulled boat's English name comes from the Tamil 'kattumaram', meaning tied wood?
note: Tamil fishermen lashed logs together to build these sturdy boats.

q: Which English word for a spiced sauce dish comes from the Tamil 'kari'?
note: Hannah Glasse's 1747 cookbook has one of the earliest English recipes for it.

q: Which big cat's English name comes from the Sanskrit 'chitraka', meaning spotted?
note: The word entered English through Hindi in the early 1700s.

q: Which British slang word meaning genuine or first-rate comes from a Hindi word for 'cooked' or 'ripe'?
note: In India a solid brick-and-cement house is still called a pucca house.

q: Which old British nickname for Britain comes from the Hindustani 'vilayati', meaning from abroad?
note: British soldiers used it to mean home; a 'Blighty wound' was one serious enough to be sent back.

q: Which British slang for 'a quick look' comes from the Hindi 'dekho'?
note: Hindi 'dekho' means 'look!', from 'dekhna', to see.

q: Which English word for a short note or voucher comes from the Hindi 'chitthi'?
note: It entered English in the late 1700s through Anglo-Indian usage.

q: Which flared riding trousers are named after a city in Rajasthan?
note: Sir Pratap Singh helped make them fashionable in England in the late 1800s.

q: Which puckered striped fabric gets its name, via Hindi, from Persian words for 'milk and sugar'?
note: The name reflects its mix of smooth and crinkled stripes.

q: Which strong timber's English name comes from the Malayalam 'tekka'?
note: Its natural oils help it resist water, so it was prized for shipbuilding.

q: Which snake-fighting animal's English name comes from an Indian word, such as Marathi 'mangus'?
note: Its nerve receptors resist snake venom, helping it take on cobras.

q: Which English word for rough jute sacking comes from the Hindi 'goni'?
note: Gunny is a coarse fabric woven from jute or hemp.

q: Which small boat's English name comes from the Hindi 'dingi'?
note: Bengali, Hindi and Urdu all have 'dingi', meaning a small boat.

q: Which English word for a very rich man comes from the Hindi-Urdu 'nawab'?
note: It first meant a Mughal provincial ruler, then Britons who returned rich from India.

q: 'Dungarees' comes from the Hindi 'dungri', which was the name of what?
note: By 1868, work clothes made from it were being called dungarees.

q: The word 'bandana' comes from a Hindi word linked to which craft?
'Mango' reached English from Malayalam or Tamil through which European language?
note: Portuguese traders brought the word 'manga' to Europe.

q: The English word 'orange' traces back, via Persian and Arabic, to which language?
note: The fruit was named first; the colour took its name from the fruit.

q: Which organ can regrow to its normal size after part of it is surgically removed?
note: Up to two-thirds of a healthy liver can be removed and it still grows back.

q: What is the medical name for the 'funny bone' nerve that tingles when you knock your elbow?
note: It isn't a bone at all; the nerve simply runs close to the skin there.

q: Hiccups are sudden spasms of which dome-shaped breathing muscle?
note: The 'hic' sound comes from the vocal cords snapping shut.

q: What is the medical name for earwax?
note: It traps dust and stops the ear canal from drying out.

q: What is the vertical groove between the nose and the upper lip called?
note: Its name comes from the Greek word 'philtron'.

q: Which clear part of the eye has no blood vessels and takes its oxygen directly from the air?
note: Its lack of blood vessels is one reason corneal transplants work so well.

q: What is the smallest skeletal muscle in the human body, found in the middle ear?
note: It tightens to damp down very loud sounds before they travel deeper into the ear.

q: Roughly how long does a human red blood cell live?
note: Adults make millions of new red blood cells every second.

q: The 'tongue map' says each taste has its own zone. What is the truth?
a: All areas can sense all tastes
options: Sweet is only at the tip
Bitter is only at the back
Salt is only on the sides
All areas can sense all tastes
note: The myth grew from a misread German study published in 1901.

q: Together, your hands and feet contain roughly what share of your body's bones?
note: Each hand has 27 bones and each foot has 26.

q: The brain is about 2% of body mass. Roughly what share of the body's energy does it use?
note: Brain scans show we use all of it; the '10% of the brain' idea is a myth.

q: Roughly how many times does an adult's heart beat in a day?
note: At 70 beats a minute, that comes to over 100,000 beats a day.

q: Goldfish supposedly have a 3-second memory. What have experiments shown?
options: They have no memory at all
They remember for about a minute
note: Goldfish have been trained to respond to sounds and colours for food.

q: Which New York skyscraper is struck by lightning an average of 23 times a year, busting 'lightning never strikes twice'?
note: Tall, pointed buildings get hit again and again because they offer the easiest path.

q: China's first astronaut said after his flight that he could not see which landmark from orbit?
note: The wall is very long but only a few metres wide, and it blends into the land.

q: What really makes a bull charge at a matador's cape?
note: Cattle are red-green colour-blind; a waving cape of any colour works.

q: Ostriches don't bury their heads in sand. What are they doing when their heads dip into the ground?
note: Ostriches lay eggs in holes dug in the ground and turn them with their beaks.

q: Are bats blind?
note: Many bats also use echolocation, but no bat species is blind.

q: A camel's hump doesn't hold water. What does it mainly store?
note: Using that stored energy lets a camel go days without food.

q: Napoleon was about average height. His 'short' image partly comes from confusion between French and English what?
note: He was roughly 1.67–1.70 m, about average for a Frenchman of his day.

q: The horned Viking helmet myth was popularised by costumes for which composer's operas in 1876?
note: Archaeologists have found no evidence that Vikings wore horned helmets in battle.

q: A popular myth says Albert Einstein failed maths at school. What is true?
note: He had mastered calculus by about 15, and he denied the myth himself.

q: Big Ben is not the tower or the clock. What is it actually the name of?
note: The tower itself was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012.

q: What mainly causes Earth's seasons?
options: Earth's changing distance from the Sun
note: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.

q: Diamonds are often said to be squeezed coal. Where do most natural diamonds actually form?
note: Most formed around 150 km down, long before land plants existed.

q: What is true about the so-called 'dark side' of the Moon?
a: It gets as much sunlight as the near side
options: It gets as much sunlight as the near side
note: We only ever see one face because the Moon spins once per orbit.

q: What actually eats holes in woollen clothes?
note: Adult clothes moths don't feed at all; only the caterpillars eat fabric.

q: What colours can dogs see?
note: Dogs have two types of colour cone cells, while most humans have three.

q: How many neck vertebrae does a giraffe have?
note: That's the same number as humans, but each giraffe neck bone can be about 25 cm long.

q: A cow's stomach has how many compartments?
note: They are the rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum.

q: Which basic taste can cats not detect?
note: A faulty gene leaves cats without a working sweet-taste receptor.

q: Owls can't move their eyes. Up to about how many degrees can they turn their heads either way?
note: Their eyes are tube-shaped and fixed in place, so the neck does the work.

q: How do dolphins sleep while still surfacing to breathe?
a: Half their brain rests at a time
options: Half their brain rests at a time
note: One eye often stays open, keeping watch while the other side rests.

q: Koalas have which surprisingly human-like feature?
note: Even under a microscope, koala prints are hard to tell apart from human ones.

q: Crickets hear through ears located on which part of their body?
note: Each ear is a small drum-like membrane just below the knee.

q: Bamboo, one of the fastest-growing plants, is actually a type of what?
note: Some bamboo species can grow nearly a metre in a single day.

q: Genetically, mushrooms and other fungi are more closely related to which group?
note: Like animals, fungi can't make their own food from sunlight.

q: Why can properly sealed honey last for years without spoiling?
a: It is low in water and acidic
options: It is low in water and acidic
note: Most bacteria and moulds can't grow in something so sugary, dry and acidic.

q: Honeybees point hive-mates towards flowers using the '___ dance'. What word fills the blank?
note: Karl von Frisch shared a 1973 Nobel Prize partly for decoding it.

q: Sound travels fastest through which of these?
note: In steel, sound moves about 17 times faster than it does through air.

q: Why do you see a lightning flash before you hear its thunder?
note: Count the seconds between flash and thunder: every three seconds is roughly one kilometre.

q: Why is the Statue of Liberty green?
a: Its copper skin reacted with the air
options: Its copper skin reacted with the air
It is made of green stone
note: When it was unveiled in 1886, it had a shiny coppery colour.

q: On which planet does one full spin on its axis take longer than one trip around the Sun?
note: Venus also spins backwards, so the Sun rises in the west there.

q: Which planet spins on its side, with its axis tilted about 98 degrees?
note: William Herschel discovered it in 1781, the first planet found since ancient times.

q: Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the solar system, is on which planet?
note: It is roughly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest.

q: What is the brightest star in the night sky, apart from the Sun?
note: It is also called the Dog Star, after its constellation, the Great Dog.

q: Roughly what share of the whole solar system's mass is in the Sun?
Which planet is so light for its size that it could float on water in a giant bathtub?
The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth. By roughly how much each year?
note: Scientists measure it by bouncing lasers off reflectors placed on the Moon's surface.

q: Orbiting Earth about every 90 minutes, how many sunrises can ISS astronauts see in a day?
note: The crew keep to GMT on board to hold a regular daily routine.

q: Because Earth bulges at the equator, which Ecuadorian volcano's summit is the farthest point from Earth's centre?
note: Its peak is about 2 km farther from Earth's centre than Everest's.

q: Measured from its base on the sea floor, which of these volcanoes is taller than Mount Everest?
note: It rises roughly 10 km from the sea floor, but only about 4.2 km is above water.

q: How hot can a lightning bolt heat the air, compared with the Sun's surface?
note: That's about 28,000°C (50,000°F); the sudden blast of hot air is what makes thunder.

q: Seen from high up in an aircraft, a rainbow can form which complete shape?
note: From the ground, the horizon usually hides the lower part of the ring.

q: What is the smallest group in which there's a better-than-even chance two people share a birthday?
note: With 70 people, the chance rises above 99.9%.

q: Why was 2000 a leap year when 1900 was not?
options: Years ending in 00 are never leap years
note: The rule keeps the calendar in step with Earth's year of about 365.2422 days.

q: What is 111,111,111 multiplied by itself?
note: 11 squared is 121 and 111 squared is 12321; the pattern holds up to nine 1s.

q: The ancient Indian game 'chaturanga' is the ancestor of which board game?
note: Its pieces stood for army units: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots.

q: The name 'Himalaya' comes from Sanskrit words meaning 'abode of' what?
note: 'Hima' means snow and 'alaya' means dwelling.

q: Why do India's newer ₹100, ₹200 and ₹500 notes have raised angled lines on their edges?
a: To help people with low vision
options: To help people with low vision
note: The ₹100 and ₹200 notes have 4 such lines; the ₹500 note has 5.

q: Until diamonds were found in Brazil in the 1720s, which country was the world's main source?
note: Famous 'Golconda diamonds' took their name from the trading city where they were sold.
